summary: Defines Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution, which lets hosts resolve names on a local link when conventional DNS is unavailable. It supports DNS formats but uses a separate port and its own resolver cache. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: LLMNR lets computers on the same local network find each other by name without a name server. A computer that wants an address for a name sends the question to the local network, and the computer that owns that name answers. It only works on one link, so it is a fallback rather than a replacement for DNS.

subtitle: Finding a name on the local network when there is no DNS server to ask.

tldr.problem: On a small network with no DNS server, or on a link where the DNS server cannot be reached, a host has no way to turn a name into an address.
tldr.mechanism: LLMNR uses the DNS packet format on port 5355 and sends queries to a link-scope multicast address, so only hosts on the same link see them; the host that owns the name answers directly to the sender.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that never reached Proposed Standard because the IETF did not agree on the approach, and the RFC says LLMNR cannot replace DNS and should only be used as a fallback.

today: RFC 4795 is an Informational document from January 2007 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The IESG note records that it was originally intended for advancement as a Proposed Standard but the IETF did not achieve consensus on the approach, and that early versions were implemented and deployed before publication. The RFC itself states that LLMNR cannot be considered a substitute for DNS.

sections.title: Name Resolution Without a DNS Server
sections.content:
Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution is based on the DNS packet format and supports all current and future DNS formats, types and classes. It operates on a separate port from the Domain Name System, with a distinct resolver cache, and it is intended to enable name resolution in scenarios where conventional DNS name resolution is not possible.

Because LLMNR only operates on the local link, it cannot be considered a substitute for DNS. Link-scope multicast addresses are used to prevent propagation of LLMNR traffic across routers, which would otherwise flood the network. Queries can also be sent to a unicast address. Propagation of LLMNR packets on the local link is considered sufficient to enable name resolution in small networks, and in such networks, if a network has a gateway, it is typically able to provide DNS server configuration.

The document notes that in future it may be desirable to consider multicast name resolution with scopes beyond the link scope, which could occur if deployment is successful, if the need arises, or if multicast routing becomes ubiquitous. Expanded support might be required for mobile ad-hoc networks. Once there is experience of deployment in terms of administrative issues, usability and impact on the network, it will be possible to re-evaluate which multicast scopes are appropriate.

Service discovery in general, and the discovery of DNS servers using LLMNR in particular, is outside the scope of the document, as is name resolution over media that are not multicast capable.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism is deliberately local. Using a link-scope multicast address means a router will not carry the query any further, so the question reaches only the computers on the same wire or the same wireless cell.

sections.title: The Packet Format and Its Extra Bits
sections.content:
LLMNR queries and responses use the DNS header format, with a few differences. Implementations should send UDP queries and responses only as large as is known to be permissible without causing fragmentation, and when in doubt a maximum packet size of 512 octets should be used. They must accept UDP queries and responses as large as the smaller of the link MTU or 9194 octets, which is an Ethernet jumbo frame of 9KB, which is 9216, minus 22 octets for the header, the VLAN tag and the checksum.

Two of the header bits carry meaning specific to LLMNR. The conflict bit, C, is set within a query to indicate that the sender has received multiple responses to that query. In a response, the bit is clear if the name is considered UNIQUE, meaning only one responder is anticipated, and set otherwise. Senders do not retransmit queries with the conflict bit set, and responders must not respond to queries with that bit set, though they may start the uniqueness verification process.

The tentative bit, T, is set in a response if the responder is authoritative for the name but has not yet verified that the name is unique. A responder must ignore the bit in a query. A response with the tentative bit set is silently discarded by the sender, except in the case of a uniqueness query, in which case a conflict has been detected and the responder must resolve it.

The other header fields follow DNS. The truncation bit must not be set in a query and is ignored by a responder in one; if it is set in a response the sender should resend the query over TCP to the unicast address of the responder, and discard the UDP response if a TCP answer arrives. A responder that is authoritative but hits an error should answer with a response code of zero, no records in the answer section and the truncation bit set, which causes the query to be resent over TCP and lets the real error code be reported there. Responder and sender behaviour around the response code is strict: a query must have the response code set to zero, the response to a multicast query must have it set to zero, and a sender must silently discard a response to a multicast query with a non-zero response code. Responders must not answer with a response code of 3, meaning the name does not exist, and instead should not respond at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are DNS messages with two extra flags. One says the device has heard more than one answer and wants to know whether there is a clash; the other says the answering device has not yet checked that its own name is unique on this network.

sections.title: How a Query and a Response Work
sections.content:
LLMNR queries are sent to and received on port 5355. The IPv4 link-scope multicast address a responder listens to, and to which a sender sends queries, is 224.0.0.252. The IPv6 link-scope multicast address is FF02:0:0:0:0:0:1:3. A host is typically configured as both a sender and a responder; a host may be configured as a sender but not a responder, but a host configured as a responder must act as a sender, if only to verify the uniqueness of its names. The document does not specify how names are chosen or configured, which may happen through any mechanism, including DHCPv4 or DHCPv6.

The typical sequence of events is that the sender sends a query to the link-scope multicast addresses, unless a unicast query is indicated; a responder answers only if it is authoritative for the name in the query, and answers a multicast query with a unicast UDP response sent to the sender; and the sender then processes the response.

Upon configuring an IP address, responders typically synthesise the corresponding A, AAAA and PTR records so they can answer queries about themselves. For example, a host named host1 in the example.com domain with an IPv4 address of 192.0.2.1 and an IPv6 address of 2001:0DB8::1:2:3:FF:FE:4:5:6 might be authoritative for host1, host1.example.com, the matching reverse names in the in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa zones, and an MX record for a local mail server.

Responders must listen on UDP port 5355 on the link-scope multicast addresses and on TCP port 5355 on the unicast addresses they may use as the source of a response, and must direct responses to the port from which the query was sent. They must respond to queries for names and addresses they are authoritative for, for both forward and reverse lookups, and must not respond for names they are not authoritative for, nor using data from the LLMNR or DNS resolver cache. If a responder is authoritative for a name but the query asks for a type it does not have, it must respond with a response code of zero and an empty answer section.

Contrary to conventional DNS terminology, an LLMNR responder is authoritative only for the zone apex. The host foo.example.com is not authoritative for child.foo.example.com unless it is configured with both names. Limiting the authority scope this way prevents complications caused by two hosts holding the names for a child and a parent node, which would otherwise produce two authoritative answers to the same query.

A sender must anticipate receiving no response, because there may be no responder on the link. If no response is received, the resolver treats it as a response saying the name does not exist. When multiple valid responses arrive with the conflict bit set, they should be concatenated and treated as multiple records from one DNS server would be, but they should not be concatenated with responses that have the conflict bit clear; instead only the responses with the bit set should be returned. Since the responder may order the records to indicate preference, the sender should preserve that ordering for the application.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asking sends the question to the multicast address, and the device that owns the name answers directly to it rather than to everybody. A device answers only for the exact name it owns, not for names underneath it.

sections.title: Using LLMNR Only as a Fallback
sections.content:
By default a sender should send LLMNR queries only for single-label names, and a stub resolver supporting both DNS and LLMNR should avoid sending DNS queries for single-label names, to reduce unnecessary DNS queries. A sender should not be enabled to send a query for any name except where the security mechanisms described in the security section can be used. A query should only be sent for the originally requested name; a searchlist is not used to form additional LLMNR queries.

LLMNR is a peer-to-peer name resolution protocol, not a replacement for DNS. Where LLMNR security is not enabled, giving LLMNR a higher priority than DNS among the enabled mechanisms would allow the LLMNR cache, once poisoned, to take precedence over the DNS cache. Use of LLMNR as a primary name resolution mechanism is therefore NOT RECOMMENDED.

Instead, it is recommended that LLMNR be used as a secondary name resolution mechanism, for situations where hosts are not configured with the address of a DNS server, where the DNS server is unavailable or unreachable, where there is no DNS server authoritative for the name of a host, or where the authoritative DNS server does not have the desired records. When it is configured this way, LLMNR queries should only be sent when all of the following conditions are met: no manual or automatic DNS configuration has been performed, and all attempts to resolve the name via DNS on all interfaces have failed after exhausting the searchlist. The second condition can arise because the DNS servers did not respond, or because they responded with an authoritative name error or with an empty answer section.

LLMNR usage may be configured manually or automatically on a per-interface basis. By default, LLMNR responders should be enabled on all interfaces at all times, and where that is considered undesirable LLMNR should be disabled, so that hosts neither listen on the link-scope multicast address nor send queries to it. Where DHCPv4 or DHCPv6 is implemented, DHCP options can configure LLMNR on an interface. The LLMNR Enable Option can explicitly enable or disable the use of LLMNR on an interface, and does not determine whether or in which order DNS is used; that order can be specified with the Name Service Search Option for DHCP.

LLMNR may prove particularly useful for link-local name resolution over IPv6, because automatic IPv6 DNS configuration mechanisms are not yet widely deployed and not all DNS servers support IPv6. A dual-stack host may be configured with a DNS server address over IPv4 while remaining unconfigured for IPv6, in which case the host sends AAAA queries to the configured server over IPv4 and is still unable to resolve names over IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: LLMNR is meant to be tried when the normal name server has failed, not before it. Giving it priority would let a spoofed answer override the real one, so the guidance is to ask DNS first and only then ask the local network.

sections.title: Two Hosts With the Same Name
sections.content:
By default a responder should be configured to behave as though its name is UNIQUE on each interface where LLMNR is enabled. It is also possible to configure multiple responders to be authoritative for the same name, for example a cluster name assigned to several hosts in a cluster. An administrator can use a name resolution utility that employs LLMNR and lists both responses and responders, to diagnose this and reconfigure responders that should not respond to the same name.

Prior to sending a response with the tentative bit clear, a responder configured with a UNIQUE name must verify that no other host within the scope of LLMNR query propagation is authoritative for the same name on that interface. Uniqueness verification is carried out when the host starts up or is rebooted, wakes from sleep with the network interface inactive, is configured to respond on an interface, is configured to respond using additional UNIQUE records, or verifies the acquisition of a new IP address and configuration. To verify uniqueness, the responder sends a query with the conflict bit clear over all the protocols on which it responds, and it is recommended that the query use the type ANY.

If no response is received, the sender retransmits the query. If a response is received, the sender must check whether the source address matches the address of one of its own interfaces, and if so the response is not a conflict. If a response is received with the tentative bit clear, the responder must not use the name. If a response is received with the tentative bit set, the responder must check whether the source IP address in the response is lexicographically smaller than the source IP address in its own query, and if so must not use the name. Periodically carrying out uniqueness verification is not necessary, wastes network bandwidth, and may be detrimental, so responders should not do it.

Hosts on disjoint network links may configure the same name, and if those links are later joined or bridged together there may be several hosts on the same link trying to use the same name. To enable ongoing detection, when a sender receives multiple responses to a query it must check whether the conflict bit is clear in any of them, and if so should send another query for the same name, type and class with the conflict bit set and the potentially conflicting records in the additional section. Queries with the conflict bit set are advisory: a responder receiving one must not respond, but must verify the existence of a conflict before acting, and if the query is for a UNIQUE name it must send its own query with the conflict bit clear.

A responder must not ignore conflicts once detected and should log them. On detecting a conflict it must immediately stop using the conflicting name in response to queries received over any supported protocol, if the source IP address in the response is lexicographically smaller than the source IP address in the uniqueness verification query. After stopping the use of a name it may elect to configure a new one, though that is not required, and a host that has stopped using a name may attempt uniqueness verification again after the TTL of the conflicting response expires.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a device claims a name it asks the network whether anyone else already has it. If two devices end up with the same name, the one with the lower address gives way, so the situation resolves itself without anyone having to configure it.

sections.title: Security on a Shared Link
sections.content:
LLMNR is a peer-to-peer protocol designed for use on the local link. While it limits the vulnerability of responders to off-link senders, it is possible for an off-link responder to reach a sender. In scenarios such as public hotspots, attackers can be present on the same link, and these threats are most serious in wireless networks such as IEEE 802.11, since an attacker on a wired network needs physical access while a wireless attacker may mount attacks from a distance. Link-layer security such as IEEE 802.11i can help if it is available.

An attacker may take advantage of conflict detection by allocating the same name, denying service to other responders and possibly receiving packets destined for other hosts. By logging conflicts, responders can provide forensic evidence of these attacks. An attacker may also spoof queries from a victim's address, and responders that set the hop limit or TTL to a value larger than one in a UDP response may reach the victim across the Internet. A sender can protect itself against unsolicited responses by silently discarding them.

LLMNR is designed to prevent the reception of queries sent by an off-link attacker, because responders receiving UDP queries must check that they were sent to a link-scope multicast address. It is possible that some routers do not implement link-scope multicast properly, or that link-scope addresses leak into the multicast routing system. To prevent an off-link sender from completing a TCP connection, a responder receiving a TCP reply answers with a SYN-ACK whose TTL is set to one, and the responder should set the TTL on the TCP listen socket to one so that the SYN-ACK carries it, which means the sender never receives the SYN-ACK and the connection does not complete. For UDP the hop limit may be any value, though a value of 255 is recommended for compatibility with early implementations of the IPv6 link-local addressing specification.

While it is difficult for an off-link attacker to send a query to a responder, it is possible to spoof a response, and by using a hop limit larger than one the forged response can reach the sender. Since the forged response is only accepted if it contains a matching identifier, choosing a pseudo-random identifier in queries gives some protection. When LLMNR is used as a secondary service, an attacker can mount a denial of service attack on the DNS servers and then poison the LLMNR cache by answering the LLMNR query with incorrect information. These threats exist with DNS too, but while switched networks or link-layer security may make it hard for an on-link attacker to snoop unicast DNS queries, multicast LLMNR queries reach every host on the link, which lets an on-link attacker spoof responses without having to guess the query identifier. The vulnerability can be reduced by limiting LLMNR to single-label names, or by using authentication.

Because LLMNR is peer-to-peer and often deployed where no trust model can be assumed, several security mechanisms may be used where a pre-arranged configuration is possible. Implementations may support TSIG and SIG(0); the use of TSIG to secure LLMNR based on group keys is described in a separate work, and while group keys demonstrate membership of a group, they do not protect against forgery by a member of that group. IPsec with a NULL encryption algorithm may be used to authenticate unicast queries and responses, or responses to multicast queries, most easily through a group pre-shared key in a small network without a certificate authority. Implementations may also support DNSSEC, using trust anchors or keys obtained from DNS queries, but since LLMNR does not support the delegated trust bits, an implementation must be DNSSEC-aware and support validation. Unlike the first two options, DNSSEC lets a responder demonstrate ownership of a name rather than mere membership of a trusted group, and so it protects against forgery.

Finally, in order to prevent responses to LLMNR queries from polluting the DNS cache, LLMNR implementations must use a distinct, isolated cache.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone on the same wireless network can answer a name query with a lie, so the answers have to be kept in a separate cache from the real name server's answers, and the protocol can be protected with shared keys or with the same signing used for DNS.

viz.caption: THE HEADER BITS THAT MEAN SOMETHING SPECIFIC TO LLMNR

items.label: Conflict
items.desc: Set in a query when the sender has received several responses. Responders must not answer a query with this bit set.

items.label: Tentative
items.desc: Set in a response when the responder is authoritative but has not yet verified that the name is unique.

items.label: Truncation
items.desc: Set when the message was too long. The sender should repeat the query over TCP instead.

items.label: Response code
items.desc: Zero in a query and in a response to a multicast query. A sender must discard a response with a non-zero code sent in reply to a multicast query.

items.label: Question count
items.desc: A sender puts exactly one question in a query, and both sides silently discard anything else.

items.title: As a fallback, not a replacement
items.text: Using LLMNR as a primary mechanism is NOT RECOMMENDED, because a poisoned LLMNR cache would then take precedence over the DNS cache.

items.title: Try DNS first
items.text: LLMNR queries should only be sent when no DNS server address has been configured, and after all attempts to resolve the name over DNS on all interfaces have failed.

items.title: Single-label names only
items.text: By default a sender should query only for single-label names, and a stub resolver should avoid sending DNS queries for those names.

items.title: No search list
items.text: A query should only be sent for the originally requested name; a searchlist is not used to form additional LLMNR queries.

items.title: Keep the cache separate
items.text: LLMNR implementations must use a distinct, isolated cache, so that responses to LLMNR queries cannot pollute the DNS cache.
